title: Telling what happened
job: A four-sentence account in the past
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE LESSON OF THIS MODULE IS NOT A TENSE. Korean DROPS EVERY SUBJECT once the topic is set, and far more thoroughly than Spanish drops a pronoun. A four-sentence account names the speaker ONCE, in the first clause, and then says nothing about who is doing anything for three more sentences. A learner who repeats jeo-neun four times has written something that reads as insistent, or as a list of unrelated facts about a stranger.

-aseo/-eoseo does a second job here. L1-M9 taught it as "because"; in a narrative it also means AND THEN, for two events where the first leads into the second — sijang-e gaseo gwail-eul sasseoyo, "I went to the market and bought fruit". The neighbouring -go simply joins two events with no such link, and the pair is worth an author's minimal pair.

KOREAN HAS NO PERFECT / IMPERFECT SPLIT, which is worth saying out loud because four other courses in this repo spend their whole M10 on one. L1-M5's -eoss- covers everything English divides between the past simple and the present perfect, and it also carries a RESULT reading: gasseoyo can mean "has gone", and so is not here. That is the only subtlety, and it is one sentence's worth.

Each item is an ACCOUNT of three or four short sentences, not one long one, and the per-sentence bound applies to each sentence inside it. Nearly every word has already been met; the honest new spend is the sequencers — meonjeo, geu daeum-e, machimnae — beside L1-M10's geurigo and hajiman.

Nothing new is opened beyond that. -deon, the double past -eoss-eoss-, reported speech -dago and the plain style all stay OUT and belong to L3. A learner who can tell what happened in four sentences with no pronouns in them has everything this level promised.

sentences.display: Meonjeo ilhaesseoyo. Geu daeum-e jip-e gasseoyo.
sentences.script: 먼저 일했어요. 그 다음에 집에 갔어요.
sentences.cue: First I worked. Then I went home.
sentences.literal: first worked. that next-at house-to went

words.note: The opener of an account, and it goes at the very front. L1-M10's geurigo and this word are the two ends of a short story.
Literally 'at that next', with L1-M7's -e on the end. geu is the 'that' of geugeo, standing in front of a noun.

sentences.trap: NEITHER SENTENCE SAYS WHO. The speaker is understood from the situation and Korean simply leaves the subject out — putting jeo-neun in both would sound insistent, as though somebody had disputed it.
sentences.sound: MEON-jeo il-HAE-sseo-yo. geu DAE-eu-me JI-be GA-sseo-yo.

variations.cue: First I ate.
Then I went home.
variations.changed: the second step on its own

variations.cue: I worked first.
variations.changed: with the topic named, which an account does once at most

mistake.display: Jeo-neun meonjeo ilhaesseoyo. Jeo-neun jip-e gasseoyo.
mistake.script: 저는 먼저 일했어요. 저는 집에 갔어요.
mistake.why: An account names the speaker once at most: Meonjeo ilhaesseoyo. Geu daeum-e jip-e gasseoyo.

sentences.usage: Opening an account of a day.
sentences.mnemonic: Say who once. Then stop saying it.

sentences.cue: I went to the market and bought some fruit.

words.note: An open market rather than a shop. Going there takes -e and buying there would take -eseo, which is M4's law once more.
L1-M9's -aseo doing its second job: not 'because' here but AND THEN, where the first event leads into the second. It carries no tense of its own.

sentences.trap: -aseo carries NO TENSE. The past sits on the last verb only, and the first clause stays in its plain shape — which is one fewer thing to conjugate, not one more.

variations.cue: I went to the market and I bought fruit.
variations.changed: -go, which joins the two with no link between them

variations.cue: I went to the market and bought apples.
I bought fruit at the market.

mistake.why: -aseo takes no tense: Sijang-e gaseo gwail-eul sasseoyo.

sentences.usage: The middle of an account, where one thing leads to another.

sentences.cue: I met a friend and we watched a film.

words.note: M6's bwayo in L1-M5's past. Watching a film and seeing a person are the same verb, and M6's mannada supplies the rest of the account's shapes: mannago, mannaseo, mannasseoyo.

sentences.trap: -go joins two events and says nothing about how they are related. Swap in -aseo and the meeting becomes the reason for the film — a difference English carries with 'and then' rather than with 'and'.

variations.cue: I met a friend and then we watched a film.
variations.changed: -aseo, so the meeting leads into the film

variations.cue: I watched a film.
variations.changed: the second event on its own

variations.cue: I met a friend and we ate.

mistake.why: -go takes no tense either: Chingu-reul mannago yeonghwa-reul bwasseoyo.

sentences.usage: Telling somebody how an evening went.
sentences.mnemonic: Only the last verb carries the tense.

sentences.cue: In the end I got home.

words.note: The closer of an account, and it carries a small sense of at last — which is why it is not simply the fourth geu daeum-e.

sentences.trap: wasseoyo is 'came' and gasseoyo is 'went', and Korean picks by where the SPEAKER is now. Telling the story at home, you came home; telling it elsewhere, you went.

variations.cue: In the end I went home.
variations.changed: told from somewhere other than home

variations.cue: In the end I met my friend.
I got home.

mistake.why: A destination takes -e: Machimnae jip-e wasseoyo.

sentences.usage: Closing an account — the last thing that happened.
sentences.mnemonic: Come or go, decided by where you are standing.

sentences.cue: I was busy yesterday, so I couldn't go.

words.note: L1-M6's gada in L1-M5's past. It also carries a RESULT reading — gasseoyo can mean 'has gone', and so is not here.

sentences.trap: Here -aseo is L1-M9's 'because' and not the narrative 'and then'. Both readings are the same ending, and only the sentence tells you which — a reason clause always comes FIRST, exactly as L1-M9 said.
sentences.sound: EO-je bap-PA-seo mot GA-sseo-yo. The pp is tense.

variations.cue: I was busy, so I couldn't go.
I didn't go yesterday.
variations.changed: M8's an — a choice rather than an obstacle

variations.cue: I was tired, so I went home.
variations.changed: L1-M9's tired, in the same because-frame

mistake.why: The reason comes first: Eoje bappaseo mot gasseoyo.

sentences.usage: Apologising afterwards for not turning up.

words.note: The past of oda, which M3 already met. Like gasseoyo it carries a result: wasseoyo can mean 'has arrived, and is here'.

sentences.trap: THIS IS THE RESULT READING. gasseoyo with jigeum does not mean he went just now — it means he has gone, and so is not here. Korean's one past covers what English splits between two tenses.

variations.cue: He's just arrived.
variations.changed: coming, with the same result reading

variations.cue: He went home yesterday.
variations.changed: with a past time word, so the plain past reading

variations.cue: Mr Kim has gone home.

mistake.why: The result is the past: Jigeum jip-e gasseoyo. The progressive would mean he is on his way.

sentences.usage: Said on the phone, when the person wanted has left.

sentences.cue: First I took my medicine, then I slept.

words.note: L1-M3's linking -go, joining two events in order and carrying no tense. The last verb does all the tense work.

sentences.trap: Two verbs, one tense, and no subject anywhere. That is what a Korean account looks like, and a learner who adds jeo-neun to each half has doubled the length and lost the register.

variations.cue: I took my medicine and slept.
First I took my medicine.
I ate and then took my medicine.
variations.changed: the same verb twice, which Korean does not mind

mistake.why: -go takes no tense: Meonjeo yak-eul meokgo jasseoyo.

sentences.usage: Telling a doctor what you did.
sentences.mnemonic: Two verbs, one tense, no subject.

sentences.cue: I bought fruit at the market. It was a bit expensive.

words.note: M3's bissayo in the past — a descriptive verb takes -eoss- exactly as an action verb does, which is one system where English has two.

sentences.trap: jom is M1's softener doing narrative work: 'a bit expensive' is a complaint made gently, and dropping it makes the sentence flatly critical of whoever sold you the fruit.

variations.cue: I bought fruit at the market. It was cheap.
It was a bit expensive.
I bought apples at the market.

mistake.why: Buying happens somewhere: Sijang-eseo gwail-eul sasseoyo.

sentences.usage: An account of an errand, with a verdict on it.
sentences.mnemonic: Describing verbs take the past too.

sentences.display: Chingu-ga wasseoyo. Geurigo gachi bap-eul meogeosseoyo.
sentences.script: 친구가 왔어요. 그리고 같이 밥을 먹었어요.
sentences.cue: A friend came. And we ate together.
sentences.literal: friend-subject came. and together rice-object ate

words.note: M6's invitation word doing plain adverb work. Nothing in the second sentence says who 'we' are — the friend in the first sentence is still in force.

sentences.trap: The second sentence has no subject at all, and it means 'we' — the friend from the first sentence plus the speaker. Korean carries that across a full stop, which English cannot do without a pronoun.
sentences.sound: CHIN-gu-ga WA-sseo-yo. GEU-ri-go GA-chi BA-beul meo-GEO-sseo-yo.

variations.cue: A friend came.
We ate together.
variations.changed: the second half, still with no subject

variations.display: Chingu-ga wasseoyo. Hajiman gachi mot meogeosseoyo.
variations.script: 친구가 왔어요. 하지만 같이 못 먹었어요.
variations.cue: A friend came. But we couldn't eat together.

mistake.display: Chingu-ga wasseoyo. Geurigo uri-ga gachi bap-eul meogeosseoyo.
mistake.script: 친구가 왔어요. 그리고 우리가 같이 밥을 먹었어요.
mistake.why: The subject is already understood: Geurigo gachi bap-eul meogeosseoyo.

sentences.usage: Telling somebody about an evening, briefly.
sentences.mnemonic: The subject carries across the full stop.

sentences.display: Meonjeo sijang-e gaseo gwail-eul sasseoyo. Machimnae jip-e wasseoyo.
sentences.script: 먼저 시장에 가서 과일을 샀어요. 마침내 집에 왔어요.
sentences.cue: First I went to the market and bought fruit. In the end I got home.
sentences.literal: first market-to went-and-then fruit-object bought. finally house-to came

words.note: M9's gwail with the object particle. In an account the objects are named and the SUBJECT never is, which is the shape the whole module is for.

sentences.trap: Two sentences, three verbs, and not one word saying who. That is a complete Korean account, and it is what the module has been building to — the tense was never the difficulty.
sentences.sound: MEON-jeo SI-jang-e GA-seo GWA-i-reul SA-sseo-yo. ma-CHIM-nae JI-be WA-sseo-yo.

variations.cue: First I went to the market and bought fruit.
In the end I got home.

variations.display: Meonjeo sijang-e gasseoyo. Geu daeum-e jip-e wasseoyo.
variations.script: 먼저 시장에 갔어요. 그 다음에 집에 왔어요.
variations.cue: First I went to the market. Then I got home.
variations.changed: two plain steps instead of a linked one

mistake.display: Jeo-neun meonjeo sijang-e gaseo jeo-neun gwail-eul sasseoyo.
mistake.script: 저는 먼저 시장에 가서 저는 과일을 샀어요.
mistake.why: An account names the speaker once at most: Meonjeo sijang-e gaseo gwail-eul sasseoyo.

sentences.usage: A whole small story, told the way Korean tells one.
sentences.mnemonic: Three verbs. No subject. That is the lesson.
